nodes.name: Isolated, non-isolated configurations
nodes.statement: If A subset Z^d is finite and if x in A, then we say that x is exposed in A if H_A (x) > 0. We say that A is isolated if every element that is exposed in A has no neighbors in A; we say that A is non-isolated if it is not isolated. We denote by Iso_d,n and NonIso_d,n the collections of isolated and non-isolated n-element configurations in Z^d, respectively. We denote the collections of the corresponding equivalence classes of configurations by widehatIso_d,n and widehatNonIso_d,n.

nodes.statement: Theorem is a consequence of a phenomenon called collapse that HAT exhibits in two dimensions. Informally, collapse occurs when the diameter of a configuration is reduced to its logarithm over a number of steps proportional to this logarithm. When a configuration has a sufficiently large diameter in terms of n, collapse occurs with high probability in n . In other words, the diameter experiences a negative drift in the sense of a Foster--Lyapunov theorem (e.g., Theorem~2.2.4 of ), which implies that HAT is positive recurrent.

Informally, collapse occurs when the diameter of a configuration is reduced to its logarithm over a number of steps proportional to this logarithm. When a configuration has a sufficiently large diameter in terms of $n$, collapse occurs with high probability in $n$ \cite[Theorem 1.5]{calvert2021}. In other words, the diameter experiences a negative drift in the sense of a Foster--Lyapunov theorem (e.g., Theorem~2.2.4 of \cite{fayolle1995}), which implies that HAT is positive recurrent.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem \ref{trans}
nodes.statement: Let d geq 5 and n geq 4, and let V be the n-element segment \(j,0,dots,0): 1 leq j leq n\ subset Z^d. It suffices to show that widehat V is transient, since widehat V in widehatNonIso_d,n and since HAT is irreducible on widehatNonIso_d,n by Theorem~. Theorem~ implies that there is a P_V-a.s.\@ finite time theta such that diam (U_t) geq n for t geq theta. Because diam (widehat V) = n - 1 < n, this implies that there are P_V-a.s.\ finitely many returns to widehat V, hence widehat V is transient.
nodes.raw_latex:
Let $d \geq 5$ and $n \geq 4$, and let $V$ be the $n$-element segment $\{(j,0,\dots,0): 1 \leq j \leq n\} \subset \mathbb{Z}^d$. 
It suffices to show that $\widehat V$ is transient, since $\widehat V \in \mathrm{\widehat{N}onIso}_{d,n}$ and since HAT is irreducible on $\mathrm{\widehat{N}onIso}_{d,n}$ by Theorem~\ref{irred}. Theorem~\ref{fate} implies that there is a $\mathbf{P}_V$-a.s.\@ finite time $\theta$ such that $\mathrm{diam} (U_t) \geq n$ for $t \geq \theta$. Because $\mathrm{diam} (\widehat V) = n - 1 < n$, this implies that there are $\mathbf{P}_V$-a.s.\ finitely many returns to $\widehat V$, hence $\widehat V$ is transient.
nodes.clean_text: Let d geq 5 and n geq 4, and let V be the n-element segment \(j,0,dots,0): 1 leq j leq n\ subset Z^d. It suffices to show that widehat V is transient, since widehat V in widehatNonIso_d,n and since HAT is irreducible on widehatNonIso_d,n by Theorem~. Theorem~ implies that there is a P_V-a.s.\@ finite time theta such that diam (U_t) geq n for t geq theta. Because diam (widehat V) = n - 1 < n, this implies that there are P_V-a.s.\ finitely many returns to widehat V, hence widehat V is transient.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem \ref{fate}
nodes.statement: Fix d geq 5 and n geq 4. Let alpha > 0 and b geq 1 be the constants from Proposition~. Fix delta in (0,frac12). In these terms, denote g(s) = s^frac12-delta for s geq 0. Additionally, let psi be a function which, given a configuration U in Conf_d,n that has a clustering in Clust_alpha,b^bullet (U), determines one such clustering. (We use psi to ``pick'' one of potentially multiple clusterings; it is otherwise unimportant.) We define theta in terms of two sequences of random times, (tau_i)_i geq 1 and (xi_i)_i geq 0. In words, tau_i is the first time t geq xi_i-1 at which U_t has an (alpha,b) DOT clustering in Ref^times, and xi_i is the first time t > tau_i at which the natural clustering (U_t)_t geq tau_i of (U_t)_t geq tau_i with psi (U_tau_i) is not a (g(t-tau_i),b) DOT clustering of U_t. More precisely, we define xi_0 = 0 and, for i geq 1, tau_i &= inf left\t geq xi_i-1: Clust_alpha,b^bullet (U_t) cap Ref^times neq emptyset right\, and\\ xi_i &= inf left\t > tau_i: U_t notin Clust_ g(t-tau_i),b^bullet (U_t) right\. Lastly, we define theta = tau_I for I = inf \i geq 1: tau_i < infty, xi_i = infty\. By the definition of theta, is satisfied, so it remains to show that theta is P_V-a.s.\@ finite for every V in Conf_d,n. Let J =inf \j : xi_j = infty\. For every V in Conf_d,n, we have P_V (theta < infty) = P_V (I < infty) = P_V (J < infty). The first equality follows from the definitions of I and theta. The second equality follows from the fact that P_V (tau_i < infty mid xi_i-1 < infty) = 1, which is a simple consequence of Theorem~. To bound the tail probabilities of J, we write P_V (J > j+1 \,|\, J > j) = fracE_V big[ P_U_tau_j (xi_1 < infty); J > jbig]P_V (J > j) leq frac34. The equality follows from the strong Markov property applied at time xi_j and the fact that P_U_xi_j (tau_1 < infty) = 1. The inequality is due to Proposition~, which implies that P_U_tau_j (xi_1 < infty) is at most frac34. The bound implies that P_V (J > j) is summable, so the Borel-Cantelli lemma implies that J is P_V-a.s.\@ finite, which by implies the same of theta.

nodes.statement: The proof of Proposition has two main steps. First, we prove that, when DOTs are a separated in d geq 5 dimensions, HAT approximates a related process, called intracluster HAT, in which transport occurs only to the cluster at which activation occurred, over a^2 steps, up to an error of O(a^-1 log (a)). Second, we show that over a^2 steps of IHAT, the separation between every pair of clusters effectively doubles, except with a probability of O(a^-1). We show this by considering the pairwise differences between representative elements of each cluster, viewed at consecutive times of return to certain, ``reference'' DOTs. Viewed in this way, the pairwise differences are d-dimensional (symmetric, but not simple) random walks. We then apply the same argument with 2a in the place of a, then 4a in the place of 2a, and so on. Each time the separation doubles, the approximation and exception errors halve, which implies that if a is sufficiently large, then the separation grows without bound, with positive probability.
nodes.raw_latex:
The proof of Proposition \ref{inf xi} has two main steps. First, we prove that, when DOTs are $a$ separated in $d \geq 5$ dimensions, HAT approximates a related process, called {\em intracluster HAT}, in which transport occurs only to the cluster at which activation occurred, over $a^2$ steps, up to an error of $O(a^{-1} \log (a))$. Second, we show that over $a^2$ steps of IHAT, the separation between every pair of clusters effectively doubles, except with a probability of $O(a^{-1})$. We show this by considering the pairwise differences between representative elements of each cluster, viewed at consecutive times of return to certain, ``reference'' DOTs. Viewed in this way, the pairwise differences are $d$-dimensional (symmetric, but not simple) random walks. 
We then apply the same argument with $2a$ in the place of $a$, then $4a$ in the place of $2a$, and so on. Each time the separation doubles, the approximation and exception errors halve, which implies that if $a$ is sufficiently large, then the separation grows without bound, with positive probability.

First, we prove that, when DOTs are a separated in d geq 5 dimensions, HAT approximates a related process, called intracluster HAT, in which transport occurs only to the cluster at which activation occurred, over a^2 steps, up to an error of O(a^-1 log (a)). Second, we show that over a^2 steps of IHAT, the separation between every pair of clusters effectively doubles, except with a probability of O(a^-1). We show this by considering the pairwise differences between representative elements of each cluster, viewed at consecutive times of return to certain, ``reference'' DOTs. Viewed in this way, the pairwise differences are d-dimensional (symmetric, but not simple) random walks. We then apply the same argument with 2a in the place of a, then 4a in the place of 2a, and so on. Each time the separation doubles, the approximation and exception errors halve, which implies that if a is sufficiently large, then the separation grows without bound, with positive probability.

nodes.statement: Define the escape probability of a finite set A subset Z^d by \[ esc_A (x) = P_x (tau_A = infty) \ 1 (x in A), x in Z^d. \] Further define the capacity of A by \[ cap_A = sum_x in A esc_A (x). \] The harmonic measure of A equals H_A (x) = fracesc_A (x)cap_A, x in Z^d.
nodes.raw_latex:
Define the escape probability of a finite set $A \subset \mathbb{Z}^d$ by
\[
\mathrm{esc}_A (x) = \mathbb{P}_x (\tau_A = \infty) \ \mathbf{1} (x \in A), \quad x \in \mathbb{Z}^d.
\]
Further define the capacity of $A$ by
\[
\mathrm{cap}_A = \sum_{x \in A} \mathrm{esc}_A (x).
\]
The harmonic measure of $A$ equals
\begin{equation*}
\mathbb{H}_A (x) = \frac{\mathrm{esc}_A (x)}{\mathrm{cap}_A}, \quad x \in \mathbb{Z}^d.

\[
\mathbb{P}_x (\tau_{y_1} < \infty) \leq \mathbb{P}_x (\tau_A < \infty) \leq |A| \, \mathbb{P}_x (\tau_{y_2} < \infty).
\]
If $\mathrm{dist} (x,A) \in [1,\kappa)$, then \eqref{eq simple set hit lb} holds because $\mathbb{P}_x (\tau_{y_1} < \infty) \gtrsim 1$. If $\mathrm{dist} (x,A) \geq \kappa$, then \eqref{eq simple set hit lb} holds because
\[
\mathbb{P}_x (\tau_{y_1} < \infty) = \frac{G(x-y_1)}{G(o)} \stackrel{\eqref{eq green asymp}}{\asymp} \|x-{y_1}\|^{2-d} = \mathrm{dist}(x,A)^{2-d},
\]
while \eqref{eq simple set hit ub} holds because
\[
\mathbb{P}_x (\tau_{y_2} < \infty) = \frac{G(x-y_2)}{G(o)} \stackrel{\eqref{eq green asymp}}{\asymp} \|x-y_2\|^{2-d} \leq \mathrm{dist}(x,A)^{2-d}.
\]
The first equality in the two preceding displays is a standard identity; see, e.g., \cite[Equation 3.4]{popov2021}.

nodes.statement: Montroll expresses G_d (o) in terms of I_0, the modified Bessel function of the first kind, as \[ G_d(o) = int_0^infty e^-t I_0 Big( fractd Big)^d d t.\] According to the integral representation of I_0 , I_0 (fractd)^d is the L^frac1d norm of e^t cos theta with respect to the probability measure pi^-1 d theta on [0,pi]: \[ I_0 Big(fractdBig)^d = left(frac1pi int_0^pi e^tfract cos thetad d theta right)^d.\] If d_1 leq d_2, then the L^frac1d_2 norm is no larger than the L^frac1d_1 norm, hence \[ G_d_1 (o) geq int_0^infty e^-t I_0 Big(fractd_2Big)^d_2 d t = G_d_2 (o).\]
nodes.raw_latex:
Montroll \cite[Eq. (2.10)]{montroll1956} expresses $G_d (o)$ in terms of $I_0$, the modified Bessel function of the first kind, as
\[ G_d(o) = \int_0^\infty e^{-t} I_0 \Big( \frac{t}{d} \Big)^d d t.\]
According to the integral representation of $I_0$ \cite[Eq. 9.6.19]{abramowitz1964}, $I_0 (\frac{t}{d})^d$ is the $L^{\frac{1}{d}}$ norm of $e^{t \cos \theta}$ with respect to the probability measure $\pi^{-1} d \theta$ on $[0,\pi]$:
\[ I_0 \Big(\frac{t}{d}\Big)^d = \left(\frac{1}{\pi} \int_0^\pi e^{\tfrac{t \cos \theta}{d}} d \theta \right)^d.\]
If $d_1 \leq d_2$, then the $L^{\frac{1}{d_2}}$ norm is no larger than the $L^{\frac{1}{d_1}}$ norm, hence
\[ G_{d_1} (o) \geq \int_0^\infty e^{-t} I_0 \Big(\frac{t}{d_2}\Big)^{d_2} d t = G_{d_2} (o).\]

Let $x \in U$. We can express $\mathrm{esc}_U (x)$ in terms of $N = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \mathbf{1} (S_j \in U)$, the number of returns made to $U$ by random walk, as 
\begin{equation}\label{esv bd1}
\mathrm{esc}_U (x) = \mathbb{P}_x (N=0) = 1 - \frac{\mathbb{E}_x [N]}{\mathbb{E}_x [N \mid N > 0]}.
\end{equation}

To bound above $\mathbb{E}_x [N]$, we note that
\begin{equation}\label{esv bd1a}
\mathbb{E}_x [N] = \sum_{y \in U} G(x-y) - 1.
\end{equation}
Since $x \in U$ and $|U| \leq 4$, there are $u, v, w\in \mathbb{Z}^d$ such that
\[
\{x - y: y \in U\} \subseteq \{o, u, v, w\} \quad \text{and} \quad \exists k,l, m \in \{1,\dots,d\}: u \succeq e_k, \,\, v \succeq e_l, \,\, w \succeq e_m.
\]
Green's function is nonnegative and nonincreasing in $\succeq$ (Lemma \ref{gpart}), hence
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{y \in U} G(x-y) \leq G(o) + G(u) + G(v) + G(w) \leq G(o) + G(e_k) + G(e_l) + G(e_m).
\end{equation*}
This bound is at most $4 G(o) - 3$ because $G(e_i) = G(o) - 1$ for every $1 \leq i \leq d$ (see, e.g., \cite[Exercise 3.2]{popov2021}). By \eqref{esv bd1a}, $\mathbb{E}_x [N]$ is at most $4 G(o) - 4$.

To bound below $\mathbb{E}_x [N \mid N>0]$, we use the fact that $\mathbb{E}_z [N] \geq G(o) - 1$ for every $z \in U$, since $N$ is at least the number of times that random walk returns to $z$. Consequently, 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}_x [N \mid N > 0] & = 1 + \mathbb{E}_x \big[ \mathbb{E}_{S_{\tau_{U}}} [N] \bigm\vert \tau_{U} < \infty \big] \geq G(o).
\end{align*}

We substitute the preceding bounds into \eqref{esv bd1} to find that
\[
\mathrm{esc}_U (x) \geq 1 - \frac{4 G(o) - 4}{G(o)} = \frac{4 - 3G(o)}{G(o)}.
\]

Let $U$ and $\mathcal{P}$ satisfy the hypotheses, and let $x \in \mathcal{P}^1$ and $y \in \partial A$. We bound the probability in \eqref{help est1} as
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}_{x} (S_{\tau_A - 1} = y, \tau_{\mathcal{P}^2} < \tau_A < \infty)
&\leq \mathbb{P}_x (\tau_{\mathcal{P}^2} < \tau_A < \infty)\\ 
&\leq \mathbb{P}_x (\tau_{\mathcal{P}^2} < \infty) \max_{z \in \mathcal{P}^2} \mathbb{P}_z ( \tau_A < \infty) \lesssim |U| \mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{P})^{4-2d}.
\end{align*}
The first inequality follows from dropping the sub-event $\{S_{\tau_A-1} = y\}$; the second holds because $\max_{z \in \mathcal{P}^2} \mathbb{P}_z (\tau_A < \infty)$ bounds above the conditional hitting probability of $A$ from an arbitrarily distributed $Z$ in $\mathcal{P}^2$; the third follows from two applications of Lemma~\ref{simple set hit}, which applies because $\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{P}) \geq \kappa$, and the fact that $|\mathcal{P}^1| |\mathcal{P}^2| \leq 3 |U|$.

We bound below the probability in \eqref{help est2} using the fact (see, e.g., \cite[Exercise 3.25]{popov2021}) that there is a constant $\lambda > 1$ such that, if the distance between $u \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and a finite set $B \subset \mathbb{Z}^d$ is at least $\lambda \mathrm{diam} (B)$, then 
\begin{equation}\label{ex325}
\mathbb{P}_u (S_{\tau_B} = v \mid \tau_B < \infty) \geq \frac12 \mathbb{H}_B (v), \quad v \in B.
\end{equation}
To this end, let $B = A \cup \{y\}$ and $C = \{u \in \mathbb{Z}^d: \mathrm{dist} (u, B) \leq \lambda \mathrm{diam} (B)\}$, and note that
\begin{equation}\label{hm like bd}
\mathbb{P}_x (S_{\tau_A - 1} = y, \tau_A < \infty) \geq \frac{1}{2d} \mathbb{P}_x (\tau_{\partial C} < \tau_B < \infty, S_{\tau_B} = y).
\end{equation}
In words, the probability that the random walk steps from $y$ when it first returns to $A$ is at least the probability that it does so after hitting $\partial C$. Note that the factor of $\frac{1}{2d}$ addresses the step that the random walk takes from $y$ into $A$ to ensure that $\tau_B = \tau_A - 1$.  
The lower bound \eqref{hm like bd} factors into
\[
\frac{1}{2d} \mathbb{P}_x (\tau_{\partial C} < \tau_B) \mathbb{P}_x (\tau_B < \infty \mid \tau_{\partial C} < \tau_B) \mathbb{P}_x (S_{\tau_B} = y \mid \tau_{\partial C} < \tau_B < \infty).
\]
We address these factors in turn.

First, the probability that random walk hits $\partial C$ before returning to $B$ is at least the probability of escape from $B \cup \{x\}$, which, by Lemma~\ref{min es}, is at least $\frac{1}{5}$ because $|B \cup \{x\}| \leq |\mathcal{P}^1| + 1 \leq 4$:
\[
\mathbb{P}_x (\tau_{\partial C} < \tau_B ) \geq \mathbb{P}_x (\tau_B = \infty) \geq \mathrm{esc}_{B \cup \{x\}} (x) \geq \frac15.
\]
Note that we use $\mathrm{esc}_{B \cup \{x\}} (x)$ instead of $\mathrm{esc}_B (x)$ because if $x \neq y$, then $x \notin B$, hence $\mathrm{esc}_B (x) = 0$ by definition and the bound of Lemma~\ref{min es} does not apply. 

Second, given that the random walk hits $\partial C$ before $B$, the conditional probability that it subsequently hits $B$ satisfies
\[
\mathbb{P}_x (\tau_B < \infty \mid \tau_{\partial C} < \tau_B) \geq \min_{z \in \partial C} \mathbb{P}_z (\tau_B < \infty) \gtrsim \mathrm{diam} (B)^{2-d}.
\]
The second inequality holds by Lemma~\ref{simple set hit}, which implies that the hitting probability of $B$ from $z \in \partial C$ is $\Omega (\mathrm{dist}(z, B)^{2-d})$, and by the definition of $C$, which implies that $\mathrm{dist} (z, B) \lesssim \mathrm{diam} (B)$ for every such $z$.

Third, given that the random walk hits $\partial C$ and then $B$, the conditional hitting probability of $y$ is at least 
\[
\mathbb{P}_x (S_{\tau_B} = y \mid \tau_{\partial C} < \tau_B < \infty) \geq \min_{z \in \partial C} \mathbb{P}_z (S_{\tau_B} = y \mid \tau_B < \infty) \geq \frac12 \mathbb{H}_B (y) \geq \frac{1}{32}.
\]
The second inequality holds by \eqref{ex325}; the third by Lemma~\ref{min es}, which applies because $|B| \leq 3$.

We multiply the three preceding bounds to conclude that
\[
\frac{1}{2d} \mathbb{P}_x (\tau_{\partial C} < \tau_B < \infty, S_{\tau_B} = y) \gtrsim \mathrm{diam} (B)^{2-d}.
\]
The bound \eqref{help est2} follows from substituting this into \eqref{hm like bd}.

For t geq 0, denote \[ g(t) = maxleft\a, t^frac12 - deltaright\ and h (t) = prod_s=0^t-1 left(1 - c left( g(s)^-1 log g(s) right)^d-2 right). \] If (D_s)_s geq 0 in Grow_a,b,delta, then g(t) is a lower bound on the separation of D_t, so the Markov property and the one-step approximation (Proposition~) imply that h(t) satisfies P_C_0 left( U_s = D_s, s leq t right) geq h(t) Q_C_0 left( V_s = D_s, s leq t right). If delta < frac12 - frac1d-2, then h(t) geq 1 - o_a (1). Indeed, some simple but tedious algebra shows that, due to the condition on delta, there are constants eta = eta (d,delta) > 0 and alpha_1 = alpha_1 (d, eta) such that, if a geq alpha_1, then \[ csum_s = 0^infty left( fraclog g(s)g(s) right)^d-2 leq O left(a^-etaright). \] Here, the implicit constant depends on all parameters: b, d, n, and delta. This bound implies that h(t) decreases to a limit of h_infty = 1 - O (a^-eta) as t to infty. We apply to conclude that P_C_0 left( (U_s)_s geq 0 in Grow_a,b,delta right) &= sum P_C_0 left( U_s = D_s, s geq 0 right)\\ &= sum lim_t to infty P_C_0 left( U_s = D_s, 0 leq s leq tright)\\ &geq h_infty sum lim_t to infty Q_C_0 left( V_s = D_s, 0 leq s leq tright)\\ &= h_infty sum Q_C_0 left( V_s = D_s, s geq 0right)\\ &= h_infty Q_C_0 left( (V_s)_s geq 0 in Grow_a,b,delta right), where the sums range over (D_s)_s geq 0 in Grow_a,b,delta.

Let $\alpha_0$ and $c$ be the constants from Proposition~\ref{p to q} and assume that $a \geq \alpha_0$. For $t \geq 0$, denote 
\[
g(t) = \max\left\{a, t^{\frac12 - \delta}\right\} \quad \text{and} \quad h (t) = \prod_{s=0}^{t-1} \left(1 - c \left( g(s)^{-1} \log g(s) \right)^{d-2} \right).
\]
If $(\mathcal{D}_s)_{s \geq 0} \in \mathrm{Grow}_{a,b,\delta}$, then $g(t)$ is a lower bound on the separation of $\mathcal{D}_t$, so the Markov property and the one-step approximation (Proposition~\ref{p to q}) imply that $h(t)$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{multistep h}
\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \left( \mathcal{U}_s = \mathcal{D}_s, s \leq t \right) \geq h(t) \mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \left( \mathcal{V}_s = \mathcal{D}_s, s \leq t \right).
\end{equation}
If $\delta < \frac12 - \frac{1}{d-2}$, then $h(t) \geq 1 - o_a (1)$. Indeed, some simple but tedious algebra shows that, due to the condition on $\delta$, there are constants $\eta = \eta (d,\delta) > 0$ and $\alpha_1 = \alpha_1 (d, \eta)$ such that, if $a \geq \alpha_1$, then
\[
c\sum_{s = 0}^\infty \left( \frac{\log g(s)}{g(s)} \right)^{d-2} \leq O \left(a^{-\eta}\right).
\]
Here, the implicit constant depends on all parameters: $b$, $d$, $n$, and $\delta$. This bound implies that $h(t)$ decreases to a limit of $h_\infty = 1 - O (a^{-\eta})$ as $t \to \infty$.  

We apply \eqref{multistep h} to conclude that
\begin{align*}
\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \left( (\mathcal{U}_s)_{s \geq 0} \in \mathrm{Grow}_{a,b,\delta} \right)
&= \sum \mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \left( \mathcal{U}_s = \mathcal{D}_s, s \geq 0 \right)\\ 
&= \sum \lim_{t \to \infty} \mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \left( \mathcal{U}_s = \mathcal{D}_s, 0 \leq s \leq t\right)\\ 
&\geq h_\infty \sum \lim_{t \to \infty} \mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \left( \mathcal{V}_s = \mathcal{D}_s, 0 \leq s \leq t\right)\\ 
&= h_\infty \sum \mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \left( \mathcal{V}_s = \mathcal{D}_s, s \geq 0\right)\\ 
&= h_\infty \mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \left( (\mathcal{V}_s)_{s \geq 0} \in \mathrm{Grow}_{a,b,\delta} \right), 
\end{align*}
where the sums range over $(\mathcal{D}_s)_{s \geq 0} \in \mathrm{Grow}_{a,b,\delta}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition \ref{help for at pairs}
nodes.statement: Let x be exposed in C^i and denote the union of clusters by U = cup_j C^j. To prove that x is exposed in U, it suffices to show that there is a path from x to the boundary of \[ F = \ z in Z^d: dist (z, U ) leq 2 diam ( U ) \, \] which otherwise lies outside of U. Because x is exposed in C^i, there is a path Gamma from x to partial F, which otherwise lies outside of C^i. We modify Gamma to obtain a path that otherwise lies outside of the rest of U as well. To this end, let \[ F_j = big\ z in Z^d: dist (z,C^j) leq diam (C^j) big\, 1 leq j leq \# C. \] We make use of two facts about the F_j. Fact 1.\ Each F_j is finite and ast-connected, so each partial_vis F_j is connected by Lemma . Fact 2.\ If sep (C) is at least max\e^2b,8sqrtd\, then each partial_vis F_j is disjoint from cup_k F_k. To see why, note that any element of partial_vis F_j is within sqrtd of an element of F_j, while the distance between distinct F_j and F_k exceeds sqrtd: dist (F_j,F_k) & geq dist(C^j,C^k) - diam (C^j) - diam (C^k) - 2sqrtd\\ & geq dist (C^j,C^k) Big( 1 - frac2b log dist (C^j,C^k) + 2sqrtddist (C^j,C^k) Big) > sqrtd. The first inequality follows from the triangle inequality; the second from the fact that C is a (cdot,b) clustering; the third from the fact that the ratio is decreasing in dist (C^j, C^k), which is at least sep (C), and some simple algebra using the assumption that sep (C) geq max\e^2b,8sqrtd\. Assume that sep (C) geq max\e^2b,8sqrtd\. We will keep the part of Gamma from x until it first encounters partial_vis F_i, which otherwise avoids cup_k F_k by assumption. We denote by J the set of labels of the F_j subsequently hit by Gamma. If J is empty, then we are done. Otherwise, let ell be the label of the first of the F_j that Gamma hits, and let Gamma_u and Gamma_v be the first and last elements of Gamma which intersect partial_vis F_ell. By Fact 1, partial_vis F_ell is connected, so there is a shortest path Lambda in partial_vis F_ell from Gamma_u to Gamma_v. We then edit Gamma to form Gamma' as \[ Gamma' = big( Gamma_1, dots, Gamma_u-1, Lambda_1, dots, Lambda_|Lambda|, Gamma_v+1, dots, Gamma_|Gamma| big).\] Because Gamma_v+1 was the last element of Gamma which intersected partial_vis F_ell, Gamma' avoids F_ell. By Fact 2, Lambda avoids cup_k F_k, so if J' is the set of labels of F_j encountered by Gamma', then |J'| leq |J|-1. If J' is empty, then we are done. Otherwise, we can relabel Gamma to Gamma' and J to J' in the preceding argument to continue inductively, obtaining Gamma'' and |J''| leq |J|-2, and so on. Because |J| leq |U|, we need to modify the path at most |U| times before the resulting path to partial F does not return to cup_k F_k after reaching partial_vis F_i. In summary, we edited Gamma to obtain a path from x to partial_vis F_i and then from partial_vis F_i to partial F, which otherwise avoids U. We conclude that x is exposed in U.
nodes.raw_latex:
Let $x$ be exposed in $\mathcal{C}^i$ and denote the union of clusters by $U = \cup_j \mathcal{C}^j$. To prove that $x$ is exposed in $U$, it suffices to show that there is a path from $x$ to the boundary of 
\[
F = \{ z \in \mathbb{Z}^d: \mathrm{dist} (z, U ) \leq 2 \mathrm{diam} ( U ) \},
\]
which otherwise lies outside of $U$. 

Because $x$ is exposed in $\mathcal{C}^i$, there is a path $\Gamma$ from $x$ to $\partial F$, which otherwise lies outside of $\mathcal{C}^i$. We modify $\Gamma$ to obtain a path that otherwise lies outside of the rest of $U$ as well. To this end, let 
\[ 
F_j = \big\{ z \in \mathbb{Z}^d: \mathrm{dist} (z,\mathcal{C}^j) \leq \mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{C}^j) \big\}, \quad 1 \leq j \leq \# \mathcal{C}.
\]
We make use of two facts about the $F_j$.

{\bf Fact 1}.\ Each $F_j$ is finite and $\ast$-connected, so each $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} F_j$ is connected by Lemma \ref{kesten result}.

{\bf Fact 2}.\ If $\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{C})$ is at least $\max\{e^{2b},8\sqrt{d}\}$, then each $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} F_j$ is disjoint from $\cup_k F_k$. To see why, note that any element of $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} F_j$ is within $\sqrt{d}$ of an element of $F_j$, while the distance between distinct $F_j$ and $F_k$ exceeds $\sqrt{d}$:
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{dist} (F_j,F_k) & \geq \mathrm{dist}(\mathcal{C}^j,\mathcal{C}^k) - \mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{C}^j) - \mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{C}^k)  - 2\sqrt{d}\\ 
& \geq \mathrm{dist} (\mathcal{C}^j,\mathcal{C}^k) \Big( 1 - \frac{2b \log \mathrm{dist} (\mathcal{C}^j,\mathcal{C}^k) + 2\sqrt{d}}{\mathrm{dist} (\mathcal{C}^j,\mathcal{C}^k)} \Big) > \sqrt{d}. 
\end{align*}
The first inequality follows from the triangle inequality; the second from the fact that $\mathcal{C}$ is a $(\cdot,b)$ clustering; the third from the fact that the ratio is decreasing in $\mathrm{dist} (\mathcal{C}^j, \mathcal{C}^k)$, which is at least $\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{C})$, and some simple algebra using the assumption that $\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{C}) \geq \max\{e^{2b},8\sqrt{d}\}$.

Assume that $\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{C}) \geq \max\{e^{2b},8\sqrt{d}\}$. We will keep the part of $\Gamma$ from $x$ until it first encounters $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} F_i$, which otherwise avoids $\cup_k F_k$ by assumption. We denote by $J$ the set of labels of the $F_j$ subsequently hit by $\Gamma$. If $J$ is empty, then we are done. Otherwise, let $\ell$ be the label of the first of the $F_j$ that $\Gamma$ hits, and let $\Gamma_u$ and $\Gamma_v$ be the first and last elements of $\Gamma$ which intersect $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} F_\ell$. By Fact 1, $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} F_\ell$ is connected, so there is a shortest path $\Lambda$ in $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} F_\ell$ from $\Gamma_u$ to $\Gamma_v$. We then edit $\Gamma$ to form $\Gamma'$ as
\[ \Gamma' = \big( \Gamma_1, \dots, \Gamma_{u-1}, \Lambda_1, \dots, \Lambda_{|\Lambda|}, \Gamma_{v+1}, \dots, \Gamma_{|\Gamma|} \big).\] 
Because $\Gamma_{v+1}$ was the last element of $\Gamma$ which intersected $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} F_\ell$, $\Gamma'$ avoids $F_\ell$. By Fact 2, $\Lambda$ avoids $\cup_k F_k$, so if $J'$ is the set of labels of $F_j$ encountered by $\Gamma'$, then $|J'| \leq |J|-1$.

If $J'$ is empty, then we are done. Otherwise, we can relabel $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma'$ and $J$ to $J'$ in the preceding argument to continue inductively, obtaining $\Gamma''$ and $|J''| \leq |J|-2$, and so on. Because $|J| \leq |U|$, we need to modify the path at most $|U|$ times before the resulting path to $\partial F$ does not return to $\cup_k F_k$ after reaching $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} F_i$. In summary, we edited $\Gamma$ to obtain a path from $x$ to $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} F_i$ and then from $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} F_i$ to $\partial F$, which otherwise avoids $U$. We conclude that $x$ is exposed in $U$.

Let $a,b$ and $\mathcal{C}_0, \mathcal{C}_1$ satisfy the hypotheses, let $x \in U_0$ and $y \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ satisfy \eqref{c0 to c1 equiv}, and denote $U_1 = \cup_j \mathcal{C}_1^j$ and $i = [x]_{\mathcal{C}_0}$. Observe that 
\begin{subnumcases}{p_{U_0} (x,y) > 0 \iff}
\mathrm{esc}_{U_0} (x) > 0, \label{p.1}\\ 
\mathrm{esc}_{U_1} (y) > 0, \,\,\text{and} \label{p.2}\\ 
y \in \partial \big( U_0 {\setminus} \{x\} \big). \label{p.3}
\end{subnumcases}

Analogously, 
\begin{subnumcases}{q_{\mathcal{C}_0} (i,x,y) > 0 \iff}
\mathrm{esc}_{\mathcal{C}_0^i} (x) > 0, \label{q.1}\\ 
\mathrm{esc}_{\mathcal{C}_1^i} (y) > 0, \,\,\text{and} \label{q.2}\\ 
y \in \partial \big( \mathcal{C}_0^i {\setminus} \{x\} \big). \label{q.3}
\end{subnumcases}
We claim that 
\[
\eqref{p.1} \iff \eqref{q.1}, \,\, \eqref{p.2} \iff \eqref{q.2}, \,\,\text{and}\,\, \eqref{p.3} \iff \eqref{q.3},
\]
which together imply \eqref{corresp}. We address the forward implications first.

\textbf{Forward implications}. Because $x \in \mathcal{C}_0^i \subseteq U_0$ and $y \in \mathcal{C}_1^i \subseteq U_1$, 
\[
\mathrm{esc}_{U_0} (x) \leq \mathrm{esc}_{\mathcal{C}_0^i} (x) \,\,\text{and}\,\, \mathrm{esc}_{U_1} (y) \leq \mathrm{esc}_{\mathcal{C}_1^i} (y),
\] hence $\eqref{p.1} \implies \eqref{q.1}$ and $\eqref{p.2} \implies \eqref{q.2}$. Next, because $\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{C}_0) \geq a > 1$, we have
\[
\partial \big( U_0 {\setminus} \{x\} \big) = \partial \Big( \bigcup_i \mathcal{C}_0^i {\setminus} \{x\} \Big) = \bigcup_i \partial \big( \mathcal{C}_0^i {\setminus}\{x\} \big).
\]
Consequently, \eqref{p.3} implies that $y \in \partial \big( \mathcal{C}_0^j {\setminus} \{x\} \big)$ for at least one choice of $j$. In fact, $j = i$ is the only choice that works as, otherwise, we would have $\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{C}_1) = 1$. We conclude that $\eqref{p.3} \implies \eqref{q.3}$.

\textbf{Reverse implications}. Because $\mathcal{C}_0$ and $\mathcal{C}_1$ are $(a,b)$ separated for an $a$ which is at least $\max\{e^{2b},8\sqrt{d}\}$, Proposition \ref{help for at pairs} applies with $\mathcal{C}_0$ or $\mathcal{C}_1$ in the place of $\mathcal{C}$. Using it, we conclude that $\eqref{p.1} \impliedby \eqref{q.1}$ and $\eqref{p.2} \impliedby \eqref{q.2}$. The argument we used for the last forward implication applies in reverse to show that $\eqref{p.3} \impliedby \eqref{q.3}$.

The fourth inequality holds because t < xi_m+1. The preceding bound addresses the first term of . Assume that $\xi_m \leq t < \xi_{m+1}$. By \eqref{tri app both},
\begin{equation}\label{tri app}
\mathrm{dist} (\mathcal{V}_t^i, \mathcal{V}_t^j) \geq \|M_t^i - M_t^j\| - \mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{V}_t^i) - \mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{V}_t^j).
\end{equation}
To replace $M_t^i - M_t^j$ by $S_m^{i,j} = M_{\xi_m}^i - M_{\xi_m}^j$ in \eqref{tri app}, we bound the norm of their difference:
\begin{equation}\label{telesc}
M_t^i - M_t^j - (M_{\xi_m}^i - M_{\xi_m}^j) = \sum_{s = \xi_m}^{t-1} \left( M_{s+1}^i - M_{s+1}^j - (M_s^i - M_s^j) \right).
\end{equation}
Taking the norm of both sides and applying \eqref{sep by one} gives
\begin{align*}
\| M_t^i - M_t^j - (M_{\xi_m}^i - M_{\xi_m}^j) \| &\leq \sum_{s = \xi_m}^{t-1} \max \{\mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{V}_s^i), \mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{V}_s^j)\}\\ 
&\leq \sum_{s = \xi_m}^{t-1} (2+s-\xi_m) \leq \frac12 (t - \xi_m)^2 \leq \frac12 (\xi_{m+1} - \xi_m)^2.
\end{align*}
The second inequality holds because cluster diameter grows by at most one with each step and because, at time $\xi_m$, the clusters have diameters of at most $2$, since they belong to $\mathrm{Ref}$. 
The fourth inequality holds because $t < \xi_{m+1}$.

The preceding bound addresses the first term of \eqref{tri app}. To address the other terms, we use \eqref{diam by one}:
\[
\mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{V}_t^i) + \mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{V}_t^j) \leq (\xi_{m+1} - \xi_m) + \mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{V}_{\xi_m}^i) + \mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{V}_{\xi_m}^j) \leq 5 (\xi_{m+1} - \xi_m).
\] 
The second inequality holds because $\xi_{m+1} - \xi_m \geq 1$ and because, at time $\xi_m$, the clusters have diameters of at most $2$.

Substituting the preceding bounds into \eqref{tri app} gives
\[
\mathrm{dist} (\mathcal{V}_t^i, \mathcal{V}_t^j) \geq \big\| S_m^{i,j} \big\| - \frac12 (\xi_{m+1} - \xi_m)^2 - 5 (\xi_{m+1} - \xi_m).
\]
The claimed bound \eqref{eq amlg2} follows from $\xi_{m+1} - \xi_m \geq 1$.

nodes.statement: Lemma~ states that we can activate any element of any cluster of V_t with a probability of at least (16n)^-1, since each cluster has two or three elements under Q_C_0. To arrange a cluster of V_t into a reference cluster, we first ensure that it is connected, possibly by activating one or two isolated elements, and then we dictate up to two additional IHAT steps to organize the connected cluster into a line segment parallel to e_1. After addressing the first cluster of V_t, we apply the same procedure to the rest of the clusters. Consider an arbitrary cluster V_t^i. The following procedure shows that V_t+4^i in Ref with a probability of at least p^4, where p = (16n)^-1 (2d)^-4. item If there is an isolated element of V_t^i, activate it (w.p.\ geq (16n)^-1). Otherwise, ``keep'' the current cluster by transporting to wherever activation occurs (w.p.\ geq (16ncdot 2d)^-1). Repeat this step to ensure that the resulting cluster is connected. item Once the cluster V_t+2^i is connected, if it does not belong to Ref, activate any element with the least e_1 component and transport it to x+e_1, where x is any element of V_t+2^i with the greatest e_1 component (w.p.\ geq (16n)^-1 (2d)^-4). Otherwise, keep the current cluster (w.p.\ geq (16n cdot 2d)^-1). Repeat this step to ensure that V_t+4^i belongs to Ref (i.e., equals \x,x+e_1\ or \x,x+e_1,x+2e_1\ for some x in Z^d). The factors of (16n)^-1 arise from the use of Lemma~; factors of (2d)^-1 arise from dictating random walk steps during the transport component of the dynamics. We can apply this procedure to the rest of the clusters to ensure that V_t+4\#C_0 in Ref^times. Note that \# C_0 is at most fracn2. This implies that \[ Q_C_0 big( xi_1 > t + tfracn2 bigmvert xi_1 > t big) leq q\] where q = 1 - p^n/2. Continuing inductively, we find that \[ Q_C_0 big( xi_1 > t big) leq q^[frac2tn] leq q^-1 e^- gamma_1 t \] for gamma_1 = tfrac2n log tfrac1q. Since q^-1 leq 2, this implies .
nodes.raw_latex:
Lemma~\ref{hm small parts} states that we can activate any element of any cluster of $\mathcal{V}_t$ with a probability of at least $(16n)^{-1}$, since each cluster has two or three elements under $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_0}$. To arrange a cluster of $\mathcal{V}_t$ into a reference cluster, we first ensure that it is connected, possibly by activating one or two isolated elements, and then we dictate up to two additional IHAT steps to organize the connected cluster into a line segment parallel to $e_1$. After addressing the first cluster of $\mathcal{V}_t$, we apply the same procedure to the rest of the clusters.

Consider an arbitrary cluster $\mathcal{V}_t^i$. The following procedure shows that $\mathcal{V}_{t+4}^i \in \mathrm{Ref}$ with a probability of at least $p^4$, where $p = (16n)^{-1} (2d)^{-4}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If there is an isolated element of $\mathcal{V}_t^i$, activate it (w.p.\ $\geq (16n)^{-1}$). Otherwise, ``keep'' the current cluster by transporting to wherever activation occurs (w.p.\ $\geq (16n\cdot 2d)^{-1}$). Repeat this step to ensure that the resulting cluster is connected.
\item Once the cluster $\mathcal{V}_{t+2}^i$ is connected, if it does not belong to $\mathrm{Ref}$, activate any element with the least $e_1$ component and transport it to $x+e_1$, where $x$ is any element of $\mathcal{V}_{t+2}^i$ with the greatest $e_1$ component (w.p.\ $\geq (16n)^{-1} (2d)^{-4}$). Otherwise, keep the current cluster (w.p.\ $\geq (16n \cdot 2d)^{-1})$. Repeat this step to ensure that $\mathcal{V}_{t+4}^i$ belongs to $\mathrm{Ref}$ (i.e., equals $\{x,x+e_1\}$ or $\{x,x+e_1,x+2e_1\}$ for some $x \in \mathbb{Z}^d$).
\end{enumerate}
The factors of $(16n)^{-1}$ arise from the use of Lemma~\ref{hm small parts}; factors of $(2d)^{-1}$ arise from dictating random walk steps during the transport component of the dynamics.

We can apply this procedure to the rest of the clusters to ensure that $\mathcal{V}_{t+4\#\mathcal{C}_0} \in \mathrm{Ref}^\times$. Note that $\# \mathcal{C}_0$ is at most $\frac{n}{2}$. This implies that
\[ \mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \big( \xi_1 > t + \tfrac{n}{2} \bigm\vert \xi_1 > t \big) \leq q\]
where $q = 1 - p^{n/2}$. Continuing inductively, we find that
\[ \mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \big( \xi_1 > t \big) \leq q^{[\frac{2t}{n}]} \leq q^{-1} e^{- \gamma_1 t}  \]
for $\gamma_1 = \tfrac{2}{n} \log \tfrac{1}{q}$. Since $q^{-1} \leq 2$, this implies \eqref{eq xi tail}.

Define the first hitting time of a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^d$ by the random walk $(S_k^{i,j})_{k \geq 0}$ associated with IHAT by 
\[
T^{i,j}_{A} = \inf\{k \geq 0: S_k^{i,j} \in A\}.
\]
Additionally, denote by $B(r) = \{z \in \mathbb{Z}^d: \|z \| < r\}$ the discrete Euclidean ball of radius $r > 0$ centered at the origin.

Fix $d \geq 5$ and $n \geq 4$, and let $b > 0$ be the constant from Proposition~\ref{rel sep bd}. It suffices to show that, for any $\delta \in (0,\frac12 - \frac{1}{d-2})$, there is $a > 0$ such that, if $W \in \mathrm{Conf}_{d,n}$ has a clustering $\mathcal{W} \in \mathrm{Clust}_{a,b}^\bullet (W) \cap \mathrm{Ref}^\times$, then the natural clustering $(\mathcal{U}_t)_{t \geq 0}$ of $(U_t)_{t \geq 0}$ with $\mathcal{W}$ satisfies
\[
\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{W}} \left( (\mathcal{U}_t)_{t \geq 0} \in \mathrm{Grow}_{\tilde a, b, \delta} \right) \geq \frac14.
\]

To this end, fix $\varepsilon = \frac12$ in Proposition~\ref{pe to qe}, and let $\alpha > 1$ be the largest of the constants it names in Propositions~\ref{pe to qe}, \ref{rel sep bd}, and \ref{tl ntb}. Then, take $a = \alpha^{1.1}$, so that $\tilde a = a^{0.99} \geq \alpha$. By Propositions~\ref{pe to qe}, \ref{rel sep bd} and \ref{tl ntb}, we have
\[
\mathbf{P}_{\mathcal{W}} \left( (\mathcal{U}_t)_{t \geq 0} \in \mathrm{Grow}_{\tilde a, b, \delta} \right) \geq \frac12 \mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{W}} \left( (\mathcal{V}_t)_{t \geq 0} \in \mathrm{Grow}_{\tilde a, b, \delta} \right) \geq \frac12 \mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{W}} ( \mathsf{G} ) \geq \frac14.
\]
Respectively, the hypotheses of these three propositions are satisfied because $\mathcal{W} \in \mathrm{Clust}_{\tilde a,b}^\bullet$ for $\tilde a \geq \alpha$, because $b$ is as in Proposition~\ref{rel sep bd} and $a \geq \alpha$, and because $\mathcal{W} \in \mathrm{Clust}_{a,b}^\bullet \cap \mathrm{Ref}^\times$ for $a \geq \alpha$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition~\ref{rel sep bd}
nodes.statement: We need to show that there is b > 0 such that, for any delta in (0,frac12), we can take a sufficiently large to ensure that, when G occurs, \[ sep (V_s) geq tilde a, diam (V_s^i) leq b log dist(V_s^i, V_s^j), and sep (V_s) geq s^frac12 - delta, \] for every distinct pair of clusters 1 leq i < j leq \# V_0 and for every s geq 0. We address these three conditions in turn. item When G_2 occurs, sep (V_s) is at least epsilon_1 a for every s geq 0. If a is sufficiently large in terms of n, then sep (V) geq tilde a. item Let ell geq 1 and s in [t_ell-1, t_ell]. Recall that N (t) = |\m geq 1: xi_m leq t\| denotes the number of returns to Ref^times by time t. Since diameter grows at most linearly in time and since V_xi_N(s)^i in Ref has a diameter of at most 2, diam (V_s^i) leq xi_N(s)+1 - xi_N(s) + 2. We can obtain a further upper bound on diam (V_s^i) by noting that, when G_4 occurs, xi_N(s)+1 - xi_N(s) is at most kappa_ell, which is essentially log t_ell. Recall that t_ell lesssim_n (2^ell a)^2 cdot (ell log a)^4. Hence, when a is sufficiently large, \[ diam (V_s^i) lesssim_n ell + log a. \] On the other hand, when G_2 occurs, dist (V_s^i, V_s^j) geq 2^ell-1 epsilon_ell a, which implies that \[ log dist(V_s^i,V_s^j) gtrsim_n ell + log a. \] By comparing these bounds, we see that diam (V_s^i) leq b log dist (V_s^i, V_s^j) holds for all sufficiently large a, so long as b is large enough in terms of n. item Let s in [t_ell-1,t_ell], in which case s^1/2 - delta is at most t_ell^1/2 - delta lesssim (2^ell a)^1-2delta cdot (ell log a)^2-4delta. When G_2 occurs, sep (V_s) gtrsim_n frac2^ell aell log a, hence sep (V_s) is larger by a factor of roughly (2^ell a)^2delta: \[ fracsep (V_s)s^1/2-delta geq fracsep (V_s)t_ell^1/2-delta gtrsim_n frac(2^ell a)^2delta(ell log a)^3. \] Consequently, we can take a sufficiently large in terms of delta and n to ensure that sep (V_s) geq s^frac12 - delta (Figure~).
nodes.raw_latex:
We need to show that there is $b > 0$ such that, for any $\delta \in (0,\frac12)$, we can take $a$ sufficiently large to ensure that, when $\mathsf{G}$ occurs, 
\[
\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{V}_s) \geq \tilde a, \quad \mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{V}_s^i) \leq b \log \mathrm{dist}(\mathcal{V}_s^i, \mathcal{V}_s^j), \quad \text{and} \quad \mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{V}_s) \geq s^{\frac12 - \delta},
\]
for every distinct pair of clusters $1 \leq i < j \leq \# \mathcal{V}_0$ and for every $s \geq 0$. We address these three conditions in turn.

\begin{enumerate}
\item When $\mathsf{G}_2$ occurs, $\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{V}_s)$ is at least $\epsilon_1 a$ for every $s \geq 0$. If $a$ is sufficiently large in terms of $n$, then $\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{V}) \geq \tilde a$.
\item Let $\ell \geq 1$ and $s \in [t_{\ell-1}, t_\ell]$. Recall that $N (t) = |\{m \geq 1: \xi_m \leq t\}|$ denotes the number of returns to $\mathrm{Ref}^\times$ by time $t$. Since diameter grows at most linearly in time and since $\mathcal{V}_{\xi_{N(s)}}^i \in \mathrm{Ref}$ has a diameter of at most $2$,
\begin{equation}\label{xi diam bd}
\mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{V}_s^i) \leq \xi_{N(s)+1} - \xi_{N(s)} + 2.
\end{equation}
We can obtain a further upper bound on $\mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{V}_s^i)$ by noting that, when $\mathsf{G}_4$ occurs, $\xi_{N(s)+1} - \xi_{N(s)}$ is at most $\kappa_\ell$, which is essentially $\log t_\ell$. Recall that $t_\ell \lesssim_n (2^\ell a)^2 \cdot (\ell \log a)^4$. Hence, when $a$ is sufficiently large,
\[
\mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{V}_s^i) \lesssim_n \ell + \log a.
\]
On the other hand, when $\mathsf{G}_2$ occurs, $\mathrm{dist} (\mathcal{V}_s^i, \mathcal{V}_s^j) \geq 2^{\ell-1} \epsilon_\ell a$, which implies that
\[
\log \mathrm{dist}(\mathcal{V}_s^i,\mathcal{V}_s^j) \gtrsim_n \ell + \log a.
\]
By comparing these bounds, we see that $\mathrm{diam} (\mathcal{V}_s^i) \leq b \log \mathrm{dist} (\mathcal{V}_s^i, \mathcal{V}_s^j)$ holds for all sufficiently large $a$, so long as $b$ is large enough in terms of $n$.
\item Let $s \in [t_{\ell-1},t_\ell]$, in which case $s^{1/2 - \delta}$ is at most $t_\ell^{1/2 - \delta} \lesssim (2^\ell a)^{1-2\delta} \cdot (\ell \log a)^{2-4\delta}$. When $\mathsf{G}_2$ occurs, $\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{V}_s) \gtrsim_n \frac{2^\ell a}{\ell \log a}$, hence $\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{V}_s)$ is larger by a factor of roughly $(2^\ell a)^{2\delta}$:
\[
\frac{\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{V}_s)}{s^{1/2-\delta}} \geq \frac{\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{V}_s)}{t_\ell^{1/2-\delta}} \gtrsim_n \frac{(2^\ell a)^{2\delta}}{(\ell \log a)^3}.
\]
Consequently, we can take $a$ sufficiently large in terms of $\delta$ and $n$ to ensure that $\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{V}_s) \geq s^{\frac12 - \delta}$ (Figure~\ref{fig: sqrtfig}).
\end{enumerate}

Let $\alpha > 0$ be the constant named in Proposition~\ref{qg1}, let $\mathcal{C}_0 \in \mathrm{Ref}^\times$ satisfy $\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{C}_0) \geq \alpha$, and let $\ell \geq 1$. By conditioning on $\mathscr{F}_{\eta_{\ell-1}}$ and then applying Proposition~\ref{qg1}, we find that
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \Big( \mathsf{G}(\ell)^{\mathsf{c}} \cap_{m=1}^{\ell-1} \mathsf{G} (m) \Big) \leq \mathbf{E}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \, \Big[ \mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \big( \mathsf{G} (\ell)^{\mathsf{c}} \mid \mathscr{F}_{\eta_{\ell-1}} \big) \mathbf{1}_{\mathsf{G} (\ell-1)}  \Big] \leq 8\ell^{-2}. 
\end{equation*} 
Consequently,
\[
\mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \Big( \big( \cap_{\ell=1}^\infty \mathsf{G} (\ell) \big)^{\mathsf{c}} \Big) = \sum_{\ell = 1}^\infty \mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \Big( \mathsf{G}(\ell)^{\mathsf{c}} \cap_{m=1}^{\ell-1} \mathsf{G} (m) \Big) \leq \sum_{\ell=1}^\infty 8 \ell^{-2} < \frac12.
\]

Assume that $\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{C}_0) = a$ for some $a > 0$. Denote $r = 2^\ell \epsilon_\ell^{-1} a + 6 \kappa_\ell^2$. By definition,
\[
\mathsf{F}_1^{i,j} (\ell)^{\mathsf{c}} = \left\{ S_{m}^{i,j} \in B(r), \,\, N(t_{\ell-1}) < m \leq N(t_{\ell}) \right\}.
\]
Assume for the moment that, when $\mathsf{F}_4 (\ell)$ occurs, the number of steps in $\mathsf{F}_1^{i,j} (\ell)^{\mathsf{c}}$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{f4 claim}
N(t_\ell) - N(t_{\ell-1}) - 1 \geq \lambda r^2
\end{equation}
with $\lambda = \gamma_3^{-1} \log \big(\gamma_2 (8 n \ell)^2 \big)$. We use \eqref{f4 claim} to prove \eqref{t bef n eq} as
\begin{align*}
\mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \left( \mathsf{F}_1^{i,j} (\ell)^{\mathsf{c}} \cap \mathsf{F}_4 (\ell) \bigm\vert \mathscr{F}_{\eta_{\ell-1}} \right) &\leq \mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{C}_0} \left( S_{N(t_{\ell-1}) + 1 + m}^{i,j} \in B(r), \,\, 0 \leq m \leq \lambda r^2 \bigm\vert \mathscr{F}_{\eta_{\ell-1}} \right)\\ 
&= \mathbf{Q}_{\mathcal{V}_{\eta_{\ell-1}}} \left( T^{i,j}_{B(r)^{\mathsf{c}}} > \lambda r^2 \right) \leq \gamma_2 e^{-\gamma_3 \lambda}  = (8n\ell)^{-2}.
\end{align*}
The first inequality follows from the definition of $\mathsf{F}_1^{i,j} (\ell)^{\mathsf{c}}$ and the claimed bound on $N(t_\ell)-N(t_{\ell-1})-1$; the first equality is due to the strong Markov property at time $\eta_{\ell-1}$; the second inequality holds by \eqref{esc time}, which applies because $\mathcal{V}_{\eta_{\ell-1}} \in \mathrm{Ref}^\times$; and the second equality holds by the choice of $\lambda$.

The claimed bound \eqref{f4 claim} holds when $a$ is sufficiently large. Indeed, when $\mathsf{F}_4 (\ell)$ occurs, 
\[
N(t_\ell) - N(t_{\ell-1}) -1 \gtrsim \kappa_\ell^{-1} (t_\ell - t_{\ell-1}).
\]
When $a$ is sufficiently large, this lower bound is at least $(2\kappa_\ell)^{-1} t_\ell$. It therefore suffices to show that
\[

\label{def lined up}

Fix a finite set $A \subset \mathbb{Z}^d$ containing the origin, and fix two elements, $x$ and $y$, in $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} A$. Let $\{B_i\}_i$ be the collection of $\ast$-connected components of $A$. Because $A$ is finite, each $B_i$ is finite and, as each $B_i$ is also $\ast$-connected, each $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} B_i$ is connected in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ by Lemma~\ref{kesten result}.

If $\Gamma$ is the path of least length from $x$ to $y$, then this length, denoted $|\Gamma|$, satisfies 
\[
|\Gamma| \leq \sqrt{d} \mathrm{diam} (A) + 2d.
\]
Indeed, by definition, if $u \in \partial_{\mathrm{vis}} A$, then there is $v \in A$ such that $\|u-v\| \leq \sqrt{d}$. By the triangle inequality, $\mathrm{diam} (\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} A)$ is at most $\mathrm{diam} (A) + 2\sqrt{d}$, which implies the bound on $|\Gamma|$ because $|\Gamma| \leq \sqrt{d}\|x-y\|$. We will edit $\Gamma$ to obtain a potentially longer path which does not intersect $A$.

If $\Gamma$ does not intersect $A$, then we are done. Otherwise, let $i_1$ denote the label of the first $\ast$-connected component of $A$ intersected by $\Gamma$. Additionally, denote by $u$ and $v$ the first and last indices of $\Gamma$ which intersect $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} B_{i_1}$. Because $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} B_{i_1}$ is connected in $\mathbb{Z}^d$, there is a path $\Lambda$ in $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} B_{i_1}$ from $\Gamma_u$ to $\Gamma_v$. We may therefore edit $\Gamma$ to form $\Gamma'$:
\[ \Gamma' = \big( \Gamma_1, \dots, \Gamma_{u-1}, \Lambda_1, \dots, \Lambda_{|\Lambda|}, \Gamma_{v+1}, \dots, \Gamma_{|\Gamma|} \big). \]

If $\Gamma'$ does not intersect $A$, then we are done, as $\Gamma'$ is contained in the union of $\Gamma$ and $\cup_i \partial_{\mathrm{vis}} B_i$, and because $\cup_i \partial_{\mathrm{vis}} B_i$ has at most $3^d |A|$ elements. Accordingly,
\begin{equation}\label{gam length}
|\Gamma'| \leq \sqrt{d} \mathrm{diam} (A) + 2d + 3^d |A| \leq \sqrt{d}\, \mathrm{diam} (A) + 3^{d+1} |A|.
\end{equation}
Otherwise, if $\Gamma'$ intersects another $\ast$-connected component $B_{i_2}$ of $A$, we can argue in an analogous fashion to obtain a path $\Gamma''$ which intersects neither $B_{i_1}$ nor $B_{i_2}$. Like $\Gamma'$, $\Gamma''$ is contained in the union of $\Gamma$ and $\cup_i \partial_{\mathrm{vis}} B_i$ and so its length satisfies the same upper bound. By continuing inductively, we obtain a path from $x$ to $y$ with a length of at most the right-hand side of \eqref{gam length}.

The path is contained in the union of $\Gamma$ and $\cup_i \partial_{\mathrm{vis}} B_i$, which is contained in $\{z \in \mathbb{Z}^d: \|z\| \leq \mathrm{diam} (A) + \sqrt{d}\}$ because $A$ contains the origin by assumption.

First, a random walk from x reaches x-ell e_1 before returning to A cup B with a probability of at least (2d)^-ell: P_x (tau_x-ell e_1 < tau_A cup B) geq (2d)^-ell. The random walk can do so, for example, by following (x-e_1,x-2e_1,dots, x - ell e_1), which lies outside of A cup B because x is lex in A and because B is a distance of at least 2^k ell sqrtd > ell from x. The equality follows the strong Markov property applied to tau_partial F_j for each j geq 1 and the fact that P_X_j (X_j+1 in F_j) = (2d)^-1, by symmetry. Third, when \tau_partial C < tau_A cup B\ occurs, the probability that the random walk never returns to A cup B is at least the minimum of P_z (tau_A cup B = infty) over z in partial C. The distance from partial C to A cup B is at least 2^k-1 ell. By Lemma~, there is a constant ell_0 = ell_0 (d) in Z_geq 1 such that, if ell geq ell_0, then P_x (tau_A cup B = infty mid tau_X_1 < tau_partial C < tau_A cup B) geq min_z in partial C P_z left( tau_A cup B = infty right) geq 1 - n 2^-k(d-2). If n is at most 2^d-3, then choosing k=1 in results in a constant lower bound, depending on d only. Otherwise, if n exceeds 2^d-3, then we can take k to be the integer part of log_2 ((2n)^frac1d-2), in which case gives esc_A cup B (x) gtrsim n^-frac1+ log_2 (d)d-2. Because cap (A cup B) is at most n G(o)^-1, the preceding bound implies that H_A cup B (x) gtrsim n^-fracd-1 + log_2 (d)d-2. Suppose that $x$ is lex in $A$ and that there are positive integers $k$ and $\ell$ for which $\mathrm{dist} (A, B) \geq 2^k \ell \sqrt{d}$. We will bound below the probability that a random walk from $x$ escapes $A \cup B$ by bounding below the probability that it (1) takes $\ell$ steps in the $-e_1$ direction, then (2) exits a sequence of doubling cubes through their $-e_1$ directed faces until it is at least a distance of $2^{k-1} \ell$ from $A \cup B$, and (3) subsequently never returns to $A \cup B$.

First, a random walk from $x$ reaches $x-\ell e_1$ before returning to $A \cup B$ with a probability of at least $(2d)^{-\ell}$:
\begin{equation}\label{lex esc bd1}
\mathbb{P}_x (\tau_{x-\ell e_1} < \tau_{A \cup B}) \geq (2d)^{-\ell}.
\end{equation}
The random walk can do so, for example, by following $(x-e_1,x-2e_1,\dots, x - \ell e_1)$, which lies outside of $A \cup B$ because $x$ is lex in $A$ and because $B$ is a distance of at least $2^k \ell \sqrt{d} > \ell$ from $x$.

Second, for $u \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and $\ell \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$, define $Q (u,\ell)$ to be the open cube centered at $u$ and with side length $2\ell$, and denote the $-e_1$ directed face of its boundary by $F(u,\ell)$:
 \[
Q(u,\ell) = \left\{z \in \mathbb{Z}^d: \max_{1 \leq i \leq d} |z_i - u_i| < \ell \right\} \quad \text{and} \quad F(u,\ell) = \left\{z \in \partial Q (u,\ell): z_1 = \min_{v \in \partial Q (u,\ell)} v_1 \right\}.
 \]
We inductively define cube centers $X_j$, cubes $Q_j$, and faces $F_j$ according to $X_1 = x-\ell e_1$, 
\[
Q_j = Q(X_j,2^{j-1}\ell), \quad F_j = F(X_j,2^{j-1} \ell), \quad \text{and} \quad X_{j+1} = S_{\tau_{\partial Q_j}}, \quad j \geq 1.
\]
When $\cap_{i=2}^j \{X_i \in F_{i-1}\}$ occurs, $X_j$ satisfies
\[
\mathrm{dist} (A, X_j) \geq 2^{j-1} \ell \quad \text{and} \quad \mathrm{dist}(B, X_j) \geq \mathrm{dist} (A,B) - 2^{j-1} \ell \sqrt{d}, \quad j \geq 1.
\]
Since the distance between $A$ and $B$ is at least $2^k \ell \sqrt{d}$, this bound implies that
\[
\mathrm{dist} (A \cup B, X_k) \geq 2^{k-1} \ell.
\]
Hence, if $C = \{z \in \mathbb{Z}^d: \mathrm{dist}(z, A \cup B) < 2^{k-1}\ell\}$, then
\begin{equation}\label{lex esc bd2}
\mathbb{P}_{X_1} (\tau_{\partial C} < \tau_{A \cup B}) \geq \mathbb{P}_{X_1} (\cap_{j=2}^k \{X_j \in F_{j-1}\}) = (2d)^{-(k-1)}.
\end{equation}
The equality follows the strong Markov property applied to $\tau_{\partial F_{j}}$ for each $j \geq 1$ and the fact that $\mathbb{P}_{X_{j}} (X_{j+1} \in F_{j}) = (2d)^{-1}$, by symmetry.



Third, when $\{\tau_{\partial C} < \tau_{A \cup B}\}$ occurs, the probability that the random walk never returns to $A \cup B$ is at least the minimum of $\mathbb{P}_z (\tau_{A \cup B} = \infty)$ over $z \in \partial C$. The distance from $\partial C$ to $A \cup B$ is at least $2^{k-1} \ell$. By Lemma~\ref{simple set hit}, there is a constant $\ell_0 = \ell_0 (d) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ such that, if $\ell \geq \ell_0$, then  
\begin{equation}\label{lex esc bd3}
\mathbb{P}_x (\tau_{A \cup B} = \infty \mid \tau_{X_1} < \tau_{\partial C} < \tau_{A \cup B}) \geq \min_{z \in \partial C} \mathbb{P}_z \left( \tau_{A \cup B} = \infty \right) \geq 1 - n 2^{-k(d-2)}.
\end{equation}

Combining \eqref{lex esc bd1}, \eqref{lex esc bd2}, and \eqref{lex esc bd3}, and taking $\ell = \ell_0$, we find that
\begin{equation}\label{lex esc bd}
\mathrm{esc}_{A\cup B} (x) \gtrsim (2d)^{-k+1} (1 - n 2^{-k (d-2)}).
\end{equation}
If $n$ is at most $2^{d-3}$, then choosing $k=1$ in \eqref{lex esc bd} results in a constant lower bound, depending on $d$ only. Otherwise, if $n$ exceeds $2^{d-3}$, then we can take $k$ to be the integer part of $\log_2 ((2n)^{\frac{1}{d-2}})$, in which case \eqref{lex esc bd} gives
\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{esc}_{A \cup B} (x) \gtrsim n^{-\frac{1+ \log_2 (d)}{d-2}}.
\end{equation*}
Because $\mathrm{cap} (A \cup B)$ is at most $n G(o)^{-1}$, the preceding bound implies that
\begin{equation*}\label{cube bd6}
\mathbb{H}_{A \cup B} (x) \gtrsim n^{-\frac{d-1 + \log_2 (d)}{d-2}}.
\end{equation*}
We conclude the proof by setting $r = 2^{k_0}\ell_0 \sqrt{d}$, where $k_0$ is the larger of $1$ and the integer part of $\log_2 ((2n)^{\frac{1}{d-2}})$.

nodes.statement: Consider the tuple of configurations C in line 27 of algorithm A_. As every element of U is eventually treadmilled with another element, or is transported next to another element, every entry of C is connected and has two or more elements. To prove that C can be lined-up with separation r = dn^2 a, we must additionally show that C is 2r separated. Ignoring those elements that were assigned to clusters in lines 10 and 23, due to line 19, clusters i < j are separated by at least \[ 3d(n-i+1)^3 a - 3d(n-j+1)^3 a.\] Because there are at most [n/2] clusters, the preceding expression is at least \[ 3d(n/2+1)^3 a - 3d(n/2)^3 a geq 2d n^2 a + n.\] At most n elements are added to clusters by executing lines 10 and 23. Because the clusters are connected, the preceding bound implies that the pairwise separation of clusters must be at least 2r = 2dn^2a.

nodes.statement: The proof takes the form of an analysis of Algorithm A_. Denote by u_k the configuration U cup pi (C) after the ktextsuperscriptth time U cup pi (C) is changed (i.e., an element is moved) by the algorithm. Additionally, denote by M the number of times the configuration changes before the outer while loop terminates. To establish , it suffices to show that there is a sequence of times t_0 = 0 leq t_1 < t_2 < cdots < t_M leq N_1 such that u_0 = U, u_M = pi big( A_ (U,a) big), and P_u_0 big( U_t_1 = u_1, U_t_2 = u_2, dots, U_t_M = u_M big) geq p_1. We will argue that M leq n(n+1), that we can take t_M = n(n+1)r_1 for r_1 = 3dn^3 a, and that P_u_k-1 big( U_t_k = u_k big) geq q, for each k in \1,dots,M\, for a constant q = q(a,d,n) > 0. The Markov property then implies that holds with N_1 = n(n+1)r_1 and p_1 = q^n(n+1). Claim 1. We claim that M leq n(n+1). Observe that the outer and inner while loops starting on lines 2 and 5 each repeat at most n times. Indeed, U loses an element every time the outer loop repeats, which can happen no more than n times. Concerning the inner loop, no non-isolated element is made to be isolated, while, each time line 6 is executed, the isolated element ell is replaced by an element x which is non-isolated. This can happen at most n times consecutively. Accordingly, U cup pi (C) changes at most n+1 times every time the outer loop repeats, hence M leq n (n+1). Claim 2. We now claim that we can take t_M = n(n+1)r_1. It suffices to argue that, each time U cup pi (C) changes, at most r_1 steps of HAT are required to realize the change. The configuration U cup pi (C) changes due to the execution of lines 8, 10 and 11, 18 and 19, or 23 and 24. In all but one case---that of lines 18 and 19---the transition requires only one HAT step. For lines 18 and 19, at most r_1 steps are needed. Because there are at most n(n+1) changes, t_M can be taken to be n(n+1)r_1. Claim 3. We now verify by considering each way U cup pi (C) can change and by bounding below the probability that it is realized by HAT. Assume U cup pi (C) has changed k-1 times so far. item Lines 8, 10 and 11, or 23 and 24: Activation at ell and transport to x. Assume that a is sufficiently large in d and n to exceed the constant r in the statement of Lemma . Then, since ell is the lex element of U and since dist (U, pi (C)) geq a, we can apply Lemma with A = U and B = pi (C) to find that H_U cup pi (C)(ell) geq h, for a positive number h = h(d,n). By the definition of mu, x is the most likely destination of an element activated at ell. Transport from ell occurs to at most 2dn sites and so, by the pigeonhole principle, the element from ell is transported to x with a probability of at least (2dn)^-1. Together, these bounds imply that P_u_k-1 big( U_t_k = u_k big) geq h (2dn)^-1. item Lines 18 and 19: Treadmilling of \ell,y\. In the first step, we activate at y and transport to ell-e_1. While y is not lex in U, by the definition of expo, it is an exposed neighbor of ell. Because dist (U, pi (C)) geq a, if a is at least 4^d n, we can apply Lemma with A = U and B = pi (C) to conclude that H_U cup pi (C) (y) is at least c_1 h from , for a positive number c_1 = c_1 (d,n). Additionally, Lemma implies that an element activated at y is transported to ell-e_1 with a probability of at least c_2 = c_2 (d,n). Consequently, denoting \[ v_1 = big( u_k-1 cup \ell-e_1,ell\ big) setminus \ell,y\, \] we have P_u_k-1 (U_1 = v_1) geq c_1 c_2 h. Now, consider the configuration v_m resulting from starting at u_k-1 and treadmilling \ell,y\ a total of m geq 2 steps in the -e_1 direction: \[ v_m = big( u_k-1 cup \ell-me_1, ell - (m-1)e_1\ big) setminus \ell,y\.\] To obtain v_m+1, we activate at ell-(m-1)e_1 and transport to ell-(m+1)e_1. By the same reasoning as before, P_v_m big( U_1 = v_m+1 big) geq c_1c_2 h. By , , and the Markov property, P_u_k-1 big( U_t_k = u_k big) geq big(c_1 c_2 h big)^r_1. The bounds and show that, whenever U cup pi (C) changes, the change can be realized by HAT (in one or more steps) with a probability of at least \[ q = min big\ h (2dn)^-1, (c_1c_2h)^r_1 big\. \] This proves . We complete the proof by combining claims 1--3. Note that, to apply Lemma~ and Lemma~, we assumed that a was at least alpha_1 in Z_geq 1, where alpha_1 is an integer which is at least 4^d n and the constant r = r(d,n) from Lemma~.

nodes.statement: The only way that the algorithm could fail to produce L (C) is if, for some outer for loop i and inner for loop j, the assignment in line 5 is impossible. This would mean that no element of D = C^i setminus \ell_i + L_j\ was exposed in pi (C). While there must be an element of D which is exposed in C^i, the elements of C^neq i could, in principle, separate D from infty. In fact, as we argue now, this cannot occur because the clusters remain far enough apart while the algorithm runs. Each C^i remains connected while the algorithm runs, so there is a ball B_i of radius n which contains C^i. The B_i are finite and ast-connected, so each ast-visible boundary partial_vis B_i is connected by Lemma~. Moreover, each partial_vis B_i is disjoint from cup_j B_j because dist (B_i, B_j) exceeds sqrtd. This lower bound holds because the clusters are initially 2dn^2 a separated and the separation decreases by at most one with each of the n loops of the algorithm, hence \[ dist (B^i, B^j) geq dist (C^i, C^j) - diam (B_i) - diam (B_j) - n geq 2dn^2 a - 5n > sqrtd. \] The rest of the argument, which constructs an infinite path from D which otherwise avoids C, is identical to the corresponding step in the proof of Proposition~. We conclude that some element of D is exposed in pi (C), which completes the proof.

It is clear from line {\bf 5} that, since the clusters of $\mathcal{D}_0$ are line segments parallel to $e_1$, this is also true of $\mathcal{D}_M$.

Case 1. Peform the following steps. In what follows, denote r = [rad (V)]+1. item[Step 1:] ``Treadmill'' a pair of elements in the -e_1 direction for m = r + dn - 2 steps. Specifically, activate the element e_1 and transport it to -e_1, then activate the element at the origin and transport it to -2e_1, followed by activation at -e_1 and transport to -3e_1, and so on. item[Step 2:] Isolate an element outside of B(r+ dn-2). Activate the latter and transport it to the e_1, then activate the element at (n-1)e_1 and transport it to the origin. item[Step 3:] Use the induction hypothesis to form (Vsetminus\x\) cup \-m e_1\, for a particular x.
